body: The spec's headline claim and its operationalization point in opposite directions. The project promises the deterministic filter 'recovers 85-90% of the noise robustness achieved by diffusion baselines.' Robustness recovery means closing the error gap between the noisy input and the diffusion result — so 85% recovery should be CD_det ≤ CD_noisy + 0.85 × (CD_diffusion − CD_noisy), where the gap term (CD_diffusion − CD_noisy) is negative. Instead SC-002 writes CD_det ≤ CD_noisy + 0.15 × (CD_diffusion − CD_noisy), which demands only that the filter close 15% of the gap. As written, a filter that recovers a sixth of the diffusion benefit would pass the '≥85% robustness' criterion. User Story 3's acceptance scenario 1 is weaker still: it only requires the deterministic CD to fall 'within the range [noisy_baseline, diffusion_baseline]', i.e., merely no worse than doing nothing. So the three statements of the same success condition (85% in the journey, 15% in SC-002, 0% in the scenario) are inconsistent, and the acceptance tests as specified would let a near-useless filter 'pass'. Also worth noting: FR-003 says filter parameters are 'optimized on held-out validation scenes using Chamfer Distance', while the methodology sketch trains them with 'mean-squared error against clean feature representations' — a train-objective mismatch worth reconciling before implementation.
